name: Umayyad Caliphate
summary: The first hereditary caliphate, which expanded from Iberia to Central Asia and made Arabic the language of administration.

knownFor.label: Dome of the Rock
knownFor.note: An early masterpiece of Islamic architecture in Jerusalem.

knownFor.label: Great Mosque of Damascus
knownFor.note: One of the oldest great mosques.

location.value: Ruled from Damascus over an empire stretching from Iberia (Spain) and Morocco to Sindh and Transoxiana (Central Asia) at its height (c. 740).

terrain.value: Deserts, river valleys (Nile, Tigris, Euphrates, Indus) and Mediterranean coasts. Syria was the political heartland.

climate.value: Mostly arid and semi-arid, with irrigated agriculture in river valleys.
climate.source: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (3rd ed., 2016)

resources.value: Taxes and agriculture of Egypt, Iraq and Syria, plus trade and the spoils of conquest.
resources.source: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (3rd ed., 2016)

disasters.value: Recurring plague outbreaks (continuing the Plague of Justinian) hit Syria and Iraq.
disasters.source: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (3rd ed., 2016)

population.value: Not stated in Wikipedia. Muslims were still a minority of the caliphate’s population, and most subjects were Christians, Zoroastrians and Jews.

urbanisation.value: Damascus was the capital. Garrison cities such as Kufa, Basra, Fustat and Kairouan grew into major urban centres.
urbanisation.source: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (3rd ed., 2016)

disease.source: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (3rd ed., 2016)

migration.value: Arab tribal armies settled across the conquered lands. Non-Arab converts (mawali) moved into cities and armies.

economicBase.value: Agriculture taxed by the state, trade, and tribute from conquest.

tradeRoutes.value: Linked the Mediterranean, Indian Ocean and Central Asian trade worlds.
tradeRoutes.source: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (3rd ed., 2016)

moneyAndTax.value: Abd al-Malik introduced the gold dinar (693) and image-free Islamic coinage (696/697), replacing Byzantine and Persian coins. A poll tax (jizya) on non-Muslims and a land tax.

inequality.value: Arab Muslims held privileges over non-Arab converts (mawali), who were sometimes still taxed. This grievance fed the Abbasid revolution.

governmentType.value: A hereditary monarchy under a caliph, ruling a centralised state run from Damascus.

keyRulers.value: Muʿawiya I (661–680, founder). Abd al-Malik (685–705, reforms). Al-Walid I (705–715, greatest conquests). Umar II (717–720). Hisham (724–743). Marwan II (744–750, last).

succession.value: Muʿawiya named his son Yazid as heir (676), breaking with earlier practice and making the caliphate hereditary. This was very controversial.

institutions.value: Abd al-Malik made Arabic the language of administration (from about 697–705), standardised coinage, and built a postal system and a professional army registered on payrolls.

stability.value: The First Fitna (civil war, ended 661). The Second Fitna (680–692), including the death of Husayn at Karbala (680). The Third Fitna (743–747 (World History Encyclopedia; Wikipedia gives 744–750)).
stability.source: Wikipedia: Umayyad Caliphate (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox); World History Encyclopedia, Umayyad Dynasty timeline (search excerpt)

eliteConflict.value: Rivalries between Arab tribal factions (Qays and Yaman), opposition from supporters of Ali (Shiʿa) and from the Kharijites.

armyAndTech.value: Arab tribal armies, later Syrian professional troops. Perhaps about 300,000–400,000 registered soldiers in the early 8th century (estimates).

majorWars.value: Conquest of North Africa (698), Hispania (711) and Sindh (711). Transoxiana (737). Sieges of Constantinople (674–678, 717–718). Defeat at Tours/Poitiers (732).

territoryChange.value: One of the largest empires in history: about 11.1–15 million km² around 720 (Wikipedia infobox estimate range).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Byzantine Empire, the Franks, the Khazars, Turkic peoples and Tang China’s sphere.

inventions.value: Islamic coinage and administration. Monumental architecture combining Byzantine and Persian techniques.

scienceEducation.value: The beginnings of Islamic scholarship (hadith, law, Arabic grammar). The large translation movement came later under the Abbasids.
scienceEducation.source: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (3rd ed., 2016)

openness.value: Kept much Byzantine and Persian administration and staff at first, then Arabised it.

communicationTransport.value: A postal service (barid) with relay stations; roads and caravan routes from Spain to Central Asia.

religion.value: Islam was the state religion. Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians were protected subjects (dhimmi) paying jizya, and were a majority of the population for a long time.

languageWriting.value: Arabic became the official language of administration, replacing Greek, Middle Persian and Coptic (around 697–705).

artsArchitecture.value: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (completed 691/692) and the Great Mosque of Damascus. Desert palaces. A formative age for Islamic art.

socialStructure.value: Arab Muslims at the top, then non-Arab Muslims (mawali), then non-Muslim protected peoples (dhimmi), and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: An Arab-Islamic identity among the ruling class, through Arabic and Islam.
sharedIdentity.source: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (3rd ed., 2016)

dailyLife.value: Courtyard houses of stone or mud brick; bread, dates, olives and meat; desert palaces for the elite.

neighbours.value: The Byzantine Empire, Franks, Visigothic Spain (conquered), Turkic peoples, Indian kingdoms, and Tang China’s frontier.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Islam and Arabic across North Africa, Spain and Central Asia, though mass conversion took centuries.

colonisation.value: A conquering empire. Arab settlers and garrisons spread across conquered lands.

riseSignals.value: Muʿawiya won the First Fitna (661). A strong Syrian army base, effective reforms by Abd al-Malik, and continued conquests.

peakPeriod.value: Greatest extent around 720–740, under al-Walid I and Hisham. World History Encyclopedia says the empire reached its greatest extent under al-Walid I (705–715), not around 720–740.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Umayyad Caliphate (checked 5 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia, Umayyad Dynasty (search excerpt)

declineSignals.value: Overstretch and costly defeats, Arab tribal feuding, resentment among non-Arab Muslims and Shiʿa supporters, and the Third Fitna.

outcome.value: Overthrown in the Abbasid revolution (750) after the Battle of the Zab. A surviving prince, Abd al-Rahman I, founded the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba in Spain (756).

sources.value: Later Arabic histories (often written under the hostile Abbasids), coins, inscriptions, papyri and non-Muslim sources. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Kennedy (2016).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Area and army size are estimate ranges. Abbasid-era sources may be biased against the Umayyads.
